RenditionDetail.description:
One master with its pixel size — the shape the per-photo route returns.

Dimensions are NOT on RenditionItem because they are not in the database: learning them means
opening the file, and RenditionItem rides along on every feed page and library listing. This
subclass exists so the one place that needs them (the print row in the viewer, opened for a
single photo) can pay for them without putting a file read behind the feed.

post.description:
Attach — or replace — the print master of an OWNED image, from a finished resumable upload.

Takes an upload_uid rather than a multipart body so a multi-hundred-MB master gets the chunked,
resumable, progress-reporting path every other upload in this app uses. The legacy multipart
`/print` route, which writes the separate print_path column, is untouched (MEMNG-51 retires it).

Trade a handoff code plus its PKCE verifier for a device PAT.

Anonymous by construction — this is how a device gets its first credential, so requiring one
would be circular. It is also cookie-free, which is what keeps CSRF out of the picture: the
request carries no ambient authority a browser could be tricked into attaching.

Every failure is a 400 with a stable machine-readable `detail`; none of them distinguishes
"wrong" from "not yours", and all of them are terminal — the client starts a new login rather
than retrying, because a code is burned by the attempt whatever its outcome.

Revoke the presenting device token, and only that one.

A bearer may revoke ITSELF and nothing else (Decision 5): the rest of token management stays
behind a browser session, so a leaked device token can neither mint successors that outlive its
revocation nor take another device offline. A session cookie is refused here for the same
reason from the other side — the SPA revokes through `/api/pats/{id}`, which knows which token
it is talking about.

get.description:
Stream the matching memos as a zip: `<memo-uid>.md` per memo plus a manifest.

With `include_media`, each memo's attachments are carried alongside its text under
`media/<memo-uid>/`, in the rendition the `tier` names (the same tier keys the asset routes
serve). A rendition that isn't on disk is skipped and noted in the manifest.

The photo book for a tag and date range: a print-readiness manifest, or the archive itself.

Selection is `tag` (default `curated`) joined to the owner's image attachments, in memo-date
order; `from`/`to` bound the memo date and are inclusive whole days. `profile` names the single
rung the book is printed at.

**Requesting a book schedules it.** Both formats enqueue a print rendition for every member
that lacks a current one, so the first request starts the work and later requests report on it;
the enqueue is idempotent, so polling costs nothing (app/services/photobook.py:build).

`format=manifest` (the default) answers with one record per photo — the name it will carry in
the archive, whether its rendition is `ready`/`pending`/`failed`/`unavailable`, its pixel size,
and the **effective dpi** it will print at for the given `page_cm`/`max_pages` geometry, judged
against `dpi`. That is the field worth having: it names the photos a layout program will flag,
before the import rather than after it. Re-fetching it is also how progress is followed.

`format=zip` streams the ready renditions as `0001_<date>_<uid>.jpg`, numbered in book order so
a folder import lands in sequence. Photos that are not ready yet are left out and recorded in
the archive's manifest.json, exactly as the generic export treats a rendition that is missing.

get.description:
Derived tiers only (F2): ?thumbnail=true → thumb, mobile UA → mobile, video → web.
The original path stays 404, as prod is today. Visibility-gated like the memo surfaces:
anonymous callers get derived tiers of PUBLIC memos only, a PAT widens to that user's
visible set, and anything else (private, orphaned, deleted) is 404 — never 403, so the
denial does not disclose that the uid exists.
